title: Redwood discovery - reliability & fallbacks with Meridian Commerce
summary: Discovery focused on reliability, incident tolerance and fallback policies across Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployments. Customer runs payment fraud and checkout personalization with strict p99 latency goals and needs fallbacks for model outages and region failures. Action items include sending pricing/SLA, running a benchmark, and sharing security docs.
topics: Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private tradeoffs
next_steps: Sofia to send Hosted/Dedicated pricing + SLA matrix
Liam to share benchmark harness and initial scripts
Meridian to provide traffic profile and p99 targets
action_items: Sofia Martinez: Send pricing + skeleton SOW:2026-09-10
Liam O'Connor: Provide benchmark scripts and example payloads:2026-09-11

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-07 15:00 UTC | Duration 48m | Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SA), Nina (CTO Meridian), Marcus (Eng Mgr), Aisha (SRE), Evan (Security)

[00:00] Sofia: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 45 minutes, we'll focus on reliability and incident tolerance across Hosted, Dedicated and Private options; quick intros?
[00:12] Nina: Hey, Nina here, CTO at Meridian, we run checkout + personalization, high throughput spikes during sales, goal is keep p99 under 450ms for the checkout flow.
[00:21] Marcus: Marcus — engineering, we're evaluating options, main concerns are region outages and model degradations.
[00:27] Aisha: Aisha, SRE lead. We need clear fallbacks, circuit-breakers, and audit trails for compliance.
[00:33] Sofia: Great. Liam, want to start with how Redwood handles multi-region routing and fallbacks?
[00:38] Liam: Yeah, sure. So broadly we have three deployment modes — hosted API, dedicated capacity and private (VPC/on-prem). For hosted we do smart routing across regions, by default requests go to the nearest available region, and if a region is degraded we auto-failover to the next region. That failover is policy driven — you can set latency bias or cost bias.
[01:00] Nina: When you say auto-failover, is that for single-request latency or for session-level state? We use KV cache for conversational context in personalization and can't lose that.
[01:10] Priya: Good question. For stateful flows we support KV cache replication across zones in Dedicated and Private. Hosted has prefix caching and optional cross-region KV replication — there's a tradeoff: cross-region replication adds write latency but preserves KV on failover.
[01:27] Aisha: So if region A is down, do you replay requests or do you route and reconstruct the cache? How do you avoid stale suggestions?
[01:33] Liam: We do a few things. First, with prefix caching we can serve cached completions for common prefixes — that reduces failed request impact. Second, we support a model fallback chain — e.g., primary model -> smaller quantized model variant -> cached response -> degraded response template. You can order those. For KV, on Dedicated you can enable async cross-region replication so the cache is eventually consistent; for strict consistency you run Private with customer-managed replication.
[02:00] Marcus: That fallback chain — what about semantic degradation? We can't have a checkout flow return wrong attrs. Is there a way to restrict fallback types by route? Like, no model fallback on final payment confirmation, only cached or hard-fail.
[02:12] Priya: Yes, per-route policies. On the Console you configure per-route fallback policy and SLOs. For high-risk routes you can disable model fallback and instead force retry/queue to dedicated capacity, or fail open to a human flow.
[02:25] Nina: SLA numbers — we've seen vendors promise 99.9 but then there's caveats. What SLA does Redwood offer by mode?
[02:33] Sofia: For Hosted API our published availability SLA is 99.95 for regional availability, with credits for sustained outages. Dedicated can be contracted at 99.99 with reserved capacity and hot-standby in another region as an add-on. Private SLA is negotiable under enterprise contract depending on customer infra. Liam, want to add specifics?
[02:50] Liam: Yeah — and it's important to note availability vs latency SLOs. We publish p95/p99 token latency profiles per model variant; you can set latency SLOs in the Console and get alerts. For Dedicated we have guaranteed throughput commitments at target latency.
[03:05] Evan: For compliance we need audit logs and KMS. How are response/inputs logged and how long retained?
[03:11] Priya: By default Hosted keeps minimal request metadata and no PII storage unless you opt-in. For Dedicated and Private you control retention — you can ship logs to your SIEM, enable customer-managed KMS/HSM for encryption at rest, and enable full audit trails with per-token cost/latency breakdown.
[03:27] Evan: SSO integration? SAML? RBAC granularity?
[03:30] Sofia: Yes SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and role-based access controls per route. Enterprise customers can integrate with their IdP and we provide fine-grained RBAC.
[03:40] Marcus: Back to failover — how do you handle sudden capacity loss like a GPU rack fault? Does traffic queue, throttle, or fail to other model families?
[03:48] Liam: There's a few mechanisms: automatic routing to compatible model variants (lower-capacity quantized models), burst capacity from dedicated pools if configured, and circuit-breakers that start rejecting (with a 503 plus reason) when backend latency or errors exceed thresholds. You can configure auto-scaling policies and a warm-standby region for Dedicated.
[04:10] Nina: If we use Hosted initially, can we pilot with bursts to Dedicated? We don't want to rework prompts.
[04:16] Sofia: Yep — that's one of Redwood's differentiators. Same API and prompt surface across modes. We can route by policy so your integration code remains identical; we just change routing at infra level.
[04:26] Aisha: For the pilot we need to run benchmarks with our real payloads. What does the benchmark harness look like?
[04:31] Liam: We'll share a harness — it's a small Go/Python client that replays traffic with sequence length distribution, concurrency and realistic inter-arrival. It measures p50/p95/p99 latencies, token cost and throughput. We'll instrument with tracing IDs so you can correlate with your logs.
[04:46] Marcus: P99 goals — we target sub-450ms for checkout. What are your realistic p99s on Hosted for a 3-token prompt vs 256-token context model?
[04:54] Liam: For small prompts with our curated generation models, typical Hosted p99 is ~250-350ms for 8k context models in US regions. For 256-token generative contexts it can be higher; it depends on batching and tokenization. We'll include our performance profile for the exact model. Dedicated with reserved GPUs will lower variance and p99s approach p95 numbers since you avoid noisy neighbors.
[05:15] Nina: Network egress/regional costs — if you auto-failover to a different cloud region, are there egress charges?
[05:20] Priya: If cross-region failover sends traffic across cloud regions there could be egress; we surface that in cost reports and you can configure a policy to avoid cross-cloud failover if cost is a blocker.
[05:30] Evan: Any limits on encrypted traffic to customer KMS? Latency overheads?
[05:34] Liam: Using customer-managed KMS adds small latency on key retrievals at session start; we cache DEKs locally to avoid per-request KMS calls. If you require HSM signing on every response there is greater latency — we can workflow that in Private where you control HSM placement.
[05:50] Sofia: Quick interruption — Marcus, what's your timeline and success criteria for a POC?
[05:54] Marcus: We want a two-week pilot that runs during a low-traffic period, validate p99 under 500ms, and test simulated region outage to verify failover & cache behavior. If that passes, we want production roll by Nov.
[06:06] Sofia: Good. We'll propose a POC that includes Hosted baseline + Dedicated pilot with warm-standby region. Liam will run benchmarks and simulate failovers.
[06:14] Aisha: On the simulated outage — can you run a DR test where you blackout a region and we observe route failover and cache behavior?
[06:20] Liam: Yes — for Dedicated we can schedule a controlled failover test in staging. For Hosted we can simulate degraded region behavior in our test environment. We'll provide runbook steps and expected signals.
[06:30] Nina: About fallbacks again: can you throttle down to a reduced feature set instead of full degrade? E.g., keep fraud check but disable personalization for a short window.
[06:38] Priya: Yup, per-route feature flags and policy rules let you do feature-level degradation. You can prioritize critical routes like payment confirmation and degrade personalization models only.
[06:46] Marcus: Are there any caveats where model fallback can return hallucinated data that would affect payments?
[06:50] Liam: We recommend disabling model fallback for authoritative routes like payment confirmation; instead you can fall back to deterministic logic or cached canonical responses. We also support output validators — short post-processors that enforce schema or confidence thresholds and can trigger automatic retry or human review.
[07:06] Evan: We'll need the security workbook and your SOC 2 plus penetration test summary.
[07:10] Sofia: We'll attach the current security workbook and SOC 2 Type II report. For Dedicated/Private we can provide more detailed network diagrams and audit examples.
[07:18] (crosstalk)
[07:21] Nina: Ok, pricing— rough delta between Hosted and Dedicated for our throughput?
[07:25] Sofia: Hosted is usage-based per-token plus support tier. Dedicated is committed monthly capacity — unit cost is lower at scale but requires commit. We'll send a comparative matrix with break-even analysis for your expected QPS and token counts.
[07:38] Marcus: One more on observability — do you expose per-route tracing and per-token cost breakdown?
[07:42] Priya: Yes, Console exposes token-level cost, latency breakdown by model, and per-route dashboards. You can export traces to your tracing backend.
[07:51] Aisha: For action items, we also need the benchmark scripts, policy config examples, and a sample failover runbook.
[07:56] Liam: We'll include those in the POC package.
[08:00] Sofia: Great — quick recap: Redwood to send pricing + SLA matrix, security docs, benchmark harness and POC plan. Meridian to send traffic profile and pick pilot dates week of 9/14. Action owners and due dates in the notes. Any final questions?
[08:13] Nina: No, that's it. Thanks.
[08:15] Sofia: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email and attach artifacts.

End of transcript. Transcription notes: some names mis-heard (e.g., Meridian references as "Maridian" at one point), occasional filler words and overlapping talk.
